sections.title: Definitions

summary.text: Defines key terms used in the TB preventive treatment handbook, such as age groups, contact, household and close contact, index patient, high transmission setting and latent TB infection. Further definitions cover programmatic management, screening and treatment completion. It closes with a call to deliver preventive treatment to 30 million people by 2022 in line with the UN high-level meeting commitments.

sections.extract: Note: Unless otherwise specified, the definitions listed below apply to the terms as used in this handbook. They may have different meanings in other contexts. Active case finding (ACF): is synonymous with systematic screening for TB disease, although it normally implies screening that is implemented outside of health facilities. Adolescent: is a person aged 10–19 years. Adult: is a person over 19 years of age.

sections.title: Chapter 1. Introduction and approach

summary.text: Introduces the TB preventive treatment handbook, explaining that about a quarter of people worldwide are infected with M. tuberculosis and that people with HIV and contacts of TB patients are at highest risk. It places programmatic management of preventive treatment within the End TB Strategy and the 2018 UN high-level meeting targets, noting low coverage so far. It describes the handbook's purpose, intended users and approach of guiding countries through decision points. A box summarises WHO recommendations and urges governments and donors to expand access.

sections.title: Chapter 2. Identification of populations for TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Discusses which at-risk populations countries should prioritise for systematic testing and TB preventive treatment, based on infection prevalence, progression risk and transmission. It sets out the rationale and WHO recommendations for people living with HIV, including children and infants, household contacts of all ages, and clinical risk groups such as patients on dialysis or anti-TNF therapy. It also covers prisoners, health workers, migrants and other groups that may be considered case by case. The chapter ends with implementation considerations for contact investigation and a call to invest in it.

sections.extract: populations for TB preventive treatment Decision point on target populations for systematic testing and TPT Which of the at-risk populations are priority targets for the programmatic scale-up of TPT, based on your country context? The WHO guidelines on TPT recommends target populations fulfilling one or more of the following criteria for PMTPT (12): • High prevalence of TB infections • High risk of progression to TB

sections.title: Chapter 3. Ruling out TB disease before TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Explains how to rule out TB disease before starting preventive treatment, since treating active disease this way risks delays and drug resistance. It reviews the sensitivity of symptom screening in different groups and the added value of chest radiography, citing related WHO recommendations. It discusses algorithms combining symptoms, imaging and tests for people with HIV, contacts and other risk groups. It ends with practical steps such as expanding rapid diagnostics, specimen transport and standard operating procedures.

sections.extract: before TB preventive treatment Decision point on how to exclude TB disease before offering TPT How can TB disease be reliably ruled out among target populations identified for TPT? Offering TPT to someone who has TB disease can delay the resolution of disease and favour the emergence of drug resistance. Thus, excluding TB disease before initiating TPT is one of the critical steps in the preventive TB care pathway.

sections.title: Chapter 4. Testing for TB infection

summary.text: Discusses the role of the tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assays before preventive treatment, stressing there is no gold standard for TB infection. It explains how each test works, their limitations and false negatives, and when testing need not delay treatment, such as for people with HIV and young child contacts. It covers test choice, logistics and programme considerations, and includes an algorithm flowchart for deciding on preventive treatment. It ends with a call to invest in shorter regimens.

sections.extract: infection Decision point on role of TST or IGRA What is the role of testing for TB infection before starting TPT among target populations prioritized by the ministry of health? Just as excluding TB disease is a critical step before starting TPT, confirming TB infection before starting TPT may increase the certainty that individuals targeted for TPT would benefit from it. sections.title: Chapter 5. TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Covers the choice among WHO-recommended TB preventive treatment regimens, from six or nine months of isoniazid to shorter rifamycin-based options such as 3HP, 3HR, 1HP and 4R. It reviews evidence on efficacy and completion rates and explains the 2020 changes to recommended durations. It also addresses dosing, regimens for contacts of drug-resistant TB, pregnancy, children and drug interactions with antiretrovirals and other medicines. The chapter closes with guidance on people who use drugs and a call to raise demand for preventive treatment.

sections.extract: treatment Decision point on choice of TB preventive treatment Which of the WHO recommended TPT regimens should be used for different individuals in the country? sections.title: Chapter 6. Safety, management of adverse reactions and other drug-related issues in TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Addresses safety concerns that hinder scale-up of TB preventive treatment, including adverse drug reactions, monitoring and counselling. It tabulates known adverse events for isoniazid and rifamycins and details hepatotoxicity risks and their management. Further sections discuss interactions with other medicines, adherence, the durability of protection and fears that preventive treatment fosters drug resistance. It cites trial data finding no significant rise in rifampicin resistance and calls for patient support to ensure completion.

sections.extract: of adverse reactions and other drug-related issues in TB preventive treatment WHO has for long recommended the use of TPT for populations at risk of TB, particularly PLHIV and child household contacts of TB patients. However programmatic scale-up of TPT has remained limited in most high TB and HIV burden countries due to other competing priorities. sections.title: Chapter 7. Adherence to TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Chapter 7 of a WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) addresses how national programmes can help people complete their prescribed regimen. It explains that adherence depends on many personal, social and treatment-related factors and lists person-centred measures such as confidential counselling, education in the person's language, involving families and giving clear advice on side-effects. It also covers warning people that TB disease can still develop during TPT, along with options such as reminders, digital adherence technologies, shorter regimens and community support. The chapter closes by urging investment in monitoring and in digital tools for recording and reporting TPT services.

sections.title: Chapter 8. Monitoring and evaluation

summary.text: Chapter 8 of the TPT handbook sets out what data should be routinely recorded and reported, the minimum dataset for following people along the TPT cascade, and the tools for collecting it. It explains how monitoring and evaluation serve patient care, national programme management and global accountability, with examples such as counting household contacts evaluated and people completing TPT. Material on the cascade of care tracks numbers targeted, evaluated, eligible, started and completed, and explains how to estimate target populations among people living with HIV and household contacts. The chapter ends with a reminder that programmes must counsel people to make informed choices and protect them from stigma.

sections.title: Chapter 9. Ethics and TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Chapter 9 of the TPT handbook discusses ethical considerations in delivering preventive treatment to people who are not ill or infectious. It stresses weighing individual benefits against harms, limiting testing and treatment to groups at proven risk, and ensuring that taking TPT is a voluntary, informed choice grounded in human rights. It also addresses equity, confidentiality, stigma and the need for adequate communication resources so that individuals and communities can decide autonomously.

sections.title: Annex 1. List of key messages

summary.text: Annex 1 of the TPT handbook lists key messages for ministries of health and for health care workers. Messages for ministries recall commitments made at the 2018 UN High-Level Meeting on TB and the End TB Strategy targets, and present TPT as an effective intervention that substantially lowers the risk of TB disease. Messages for health workers cover shorter rifapentine- or rifampicin-based regimens, which are reported to be easier to complete, plus counselling before treatment, ruling out TB disease and managing adverse events. Notes point to funding sources and to the Global Drug Facility for medicines.

sections.title: Annex 2. Coordination mechanisms to support PMTPT

summary.text: Annex 2 recommends that ministries of health set up or strengthen a joint national coordinating body and a technical expert working group to drive scale-up of programmatic TPT management. It outlines their terms of reference, membership and secretariat arrangements, and asks TB and HIV programmes to fund regular meetings.

sections.extract: mechanisms to support PMTPT The ministry of health should create and strengthen a joint national coordinating body and/or national technical expert working group to support national scale-up of PMTPT through implementation of the latest global guidelines. sections.title: Annex 3. Costing considerations for programmatic management of TB preventive treatment

summary.text: Annex 3 lists the main cost drivers to consider when budgeting for programmatic TPT management. These include target population sizes, tests for TB infection and chest radiography, human resources, medicines and procurement, and recording and reporting systems.

sections.extract: for programmatic management of TB preventive treatment When preparing a budget for PMTPT, the following considerations need to be made given that these are major cost determinants: • Estimated burden – Populations of each target group (PLHIV, contacts, clinical risk groups, other risk groups) – Number of households and other sites (health facilities, ARV centres) to be covered for expansion of TPT activities •

sections.title: Annex 4. Planning checklist for PMTPT

summary.text: Annex 4 provides a planning checklist for programmatic TPT management, with columns for current status and next steps. Activities covered include strategic planning, guideline updates, coverage of risk groups, training, advocacy, community outreach and medicine supply and stock management.

sections.title: Annex 5. Answers to frequently asked questions on TST

summary.text: Annex 5 answers frequently asked questions about the tuberculin skin test (TST) for TB infection. It explains how the test works, the standard tuberculin doses and intradermal injection technique, and how to read and measure the induration, including the ballpoint pen method. It also covers interpreting results, causes of false-positive and false-negative readings, and the limited effect of BCG vaccination given at birth.

sections.extract: asked questions on TST What is tuberculin skin testing (139)? Tuberculin skin test (TST), first introduced in 1908, remains the most commonly used test for TB infection in the world due to its low cost and feasibility to implement in low resource settings. sections.title: Annex 6. Answers to frequently asked questions on IGRAs

summary.text: Annex 6 answers frequently asked questions about interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for TB infection, including the two commercial tests WHO reviewed in 2017. It explains that IGRAs measure interferon-gamma released by white blood cells exposed to M. tuberculosis-specific antigens absent from BCG strains, and that like TST they cannot separate infection from disease. It also covers specimen handling, interpretation and how to handle discordant or borderline results.

sections.extract: Annex 6. Answers to frequently asked questions on IGRAs What are IGRAs? Interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs) are whole-blood tests that can aid in diagnosing M. tuberculosis infection (43). Like TST, IGRAs cannot differentiate between TB infection and TB disease.
